The Archimedean Property

However small a step, repeating it eventually passes any target. That is the Archimedean property.

The reals contain no infinitely small numbers. However tiny a positive number, adding it to itself enough times outgrows any given large number. Without this fact, ε\varepsilonε-NNN arguments could never pick a "large enough NNN". The proof uses the least-upper-bound axiom.

For example, one step of an 🐜 ant is tiny. But an ant that never stops crosses a soccer field, and eventually circles the Earth. It is the count of steps, not their size, that wins.

∀a>0, ∀b∈R, ∃n∈N: na>b\forall a > 0, \ \forall b \in \mathbb{R}, \ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}: \ na > b∀a>0, ∀b∈R, ∃n∈N: na>b
∀ε>0, ∃n∈N: 1n<ε\forall \varepsilon > 0, \ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}: \ \frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon∀ε>0, ∃n∈N: n1​<ε
